questions.stem: The nucleon number of an atom is the

options.text: number of protons in the nucleus
number of electrons in a neutral atom
total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus

questions.explanation: A nucleon is a proton or a neutron. The nucleon number $A$ (also called the mass number) is the total of both. The proton number $Z$ counts protons only, and in a neutral atom $Z$ also equals the number of electrons.

distractorRationale.a: That is the proton (atomic) number Z, not A
distractorRationale.b: That also equals Z in a neutral atom; electrons are not nucleons
distractorRationale.d: Neutron number is A − Z, which is only part of the nucleon total

questions.stem: A line emission spectrum is produced when electrons in an atom

options.text: jump from a lower energy level to a higher one
jump from a higher energy level to a lower one
are stripped from the atom by a strong magnetic field

questions.explanation: A photon is emitted only when an electron loses energy by falling to a lower level. The photon energy equals the gap, $hf = E_{\text{upper}} - E_{\text{lower}}$, so only certain frequencies appear — a line spectrum. Jumping up absorbs a photon and gives an absorption line.

distractorRationale.a: An upward jump absorbs a photon; that produces an absorption spectrum, not an emission spectrum
distractorRationale.c: In Bohr's model a steady orbit does not radiate, so no spectrum is produced
distractorRationale.d: Ionisation may occur in a discharge tube, but the coloured lines come from bound electrons changing levels, not from the magnetic field

questions.stem: The nuclide ${}^{23}_{11}\mathrm{Na}$ contains
questions.explanation: The lower number is $Z = 11$ protons (and 11 electrons if the atom is neutral). The upper number is $A = 23$ nucleons, so neutrons $= A - Z = 12$. Sodium's identity is fixed by $Z = 11$; $A$ merely tells you which isotope.

distractorRationale.a: This takes A as the neutron number instead of computing A − Z
distractorRationale.c: This swaps A and Z
distractorRationale.d: This swaps proton and neutron counts

questions.stem: Calculate the energy of a photon of frequency $5.0 \times 10^{14}\ \text{Hz}$. Take $h = 6.6 \times 10^{-34}\ \text{J s}$. Give your answer in units of $10^{-19}\ \text{J}$ (so 3.3 × 10⁻¹⁹ J is entered as 3.3).
questions.explanation: $E = hf = (6.6 \times 10^{-34}) \times (5.0 \times 10^{14}) = 33 \times 10^{-20} = 3.3 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{J}$. Enter 3.3. Using $E = h/f$ would give a nonsense $10^{-48}$ figure; forgetting to add the powers of ten is the usual slip.

questions.stem: The work function of a metal is the

options.text: maximum kinetic energy of an emitted photoelectron
minimum photon energy needed to free an electron from the metal
energy of the most energetic photon in the incident beam

questions.explanation: The work function $\phi$ is the energy that must be given to the least tightly bound electron to just free it. It equals $hf_0$, where $f_0$ is the threshold frequency. Any surplus $hf - \phi$ becomes kinetic energy of the photoelectron.

distractorRationale.a: That surplus is ½mv_max², which is hf − φ, not φ itself
distractorRationale.c: The incident photon energy is hf; the work function is a property of the metal, independent of the beam
distractorRationale.d: Threshold wavelength λ₀ = c/f₀ is related to φ by φ = hc/λ₀, but φ is an energy, not a wavelength

questions.stem: Light below the threshold frequency shines on a clean metal surface. If the intensity of this light is greatly increased,

options.text: photoelectrons are emitted with greater kinetic energy
photoelectrons are emitted, but only after a time delay
the threshold frequency of the metal is lowered

questions.explanation: Each electron needs a single photon of energy at least $\phi = hf_0$. Photons below $f_0$ are individually too feeble, no matter how many of them arrive. Intensity is the number of photons per second, not their individual energy, so turning up the brightness cannot cross the threshold. This is the observation that a wave theory cannot explain.

distractorRationale.a: KE_max depends on frequency through hf − φ; below threshold there are no photoelectrons at all
distractorRationale.b: There is no delayed emission below threshold; the photoelectric effect is immediate when f > f₀ and absent when f < f₀
distractorRationale.d: The work function is a property of the metal surface, not of the brightness of the lamp

questions.stem: Radiation of frequency $1.0 \times 10^{15}\ \text{Hz}$ falls on a metal of work function $3.3 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{J}$. Taking $h = 6.6 \times 10^{-34}\ \text{J s}$, the maximum kinetic energy of a photoelectron is

options.text: zero, because the frequency is below threshold

questions.explanation: Photon energy $hf = (6.6 \times 10^{-34}) \times (1.0 \times 10^{15}) = 6.6 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{J}$. Then $KE_{\max} = hf - \phi = 6.6 \times 10^{-19} - 3.3 \times 10^{-19} = 3.3 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{J}$. Threshold frequency $f_0 = \phi / h = 5.0 \times 10^{14}\ \text{Hz}$, so this radiation is above threshold and electrons are emitted.

distractorRationale.b: That is the photon energy hf, before subtracting the work function
distractorRationale.c: That is hf + φ, adding instead of subtracting
distractorRationale.d: f₀ is 5.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz, so 1.0 × 10¹⁵ Hz is above threshold

questions.stem: An electron drops between two levels 3.3 × 10⁻¹⁹ J apart. Taking h = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J s and c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s, calculate the wavelength of the emitted photon. Give your answer in metres as a decimal (for example 6.0e-7 for 6.0 × 10⁻⁷ m).
questions.explanation: $E = hc / \lambda$, so $\lambda = hc / E = (6.6 \times 10^{-34} \times 3.0 \times 10^{8}) / (3.3 \times 10^{-19}) = (1.98 \times 10^{-25}) / (3.3 \times 10^{-19}) = 6.0 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{m}$. That is 600 nm, a visible orange-red. Using $E = h\lambda / c$ inverted would scramble the powers of ten.

questions.stem: The nuclear model of the atom was proposed by which scientist?
questions.explanation: Ernest Rutherford proposed the nuclear model of the atom in 1911, which described the atom as having a small, dense nucleus surrounded by electrons. This model was a significant advancement in atomic theory, moving away from the earlier plum pudding model.

distractorRationale.a: Albert Einstein is known for his theories of relativity, not atomic structure.
distractorRationale.b: Niels Bohr developed the Bohr model, which built on Rutherford's nuclear model.
distractorRationale.d: James Chadwick discovered the neutron, but did not propose the nuclear model.

questions.stem: In an atom, the energy levels are quantized. What does this imply?

options.text: Electrons can occupy any energy level.
Electrons can only occupy certain discrete energy levels.
Energy levels have no effect on electron behavior.

questions.explanation: The quantization of energy levels means that electrons can only exist in specific energy states and cannot have energies in between these levels. This concept is fundamental to understanding atomic structure and electron transitions.

distractorRationale.a: This statement is incorrect as it contradicts the principle of quantization.
distractorRationale.c: Energy levels are not continuous; they are discrete.
distractorRationale.d: Energy levels significantly influence electron behavior and spectral lines.

distractorRationale.b: Resonance frequency refers to the frequency at which a system oscillates naturally.
distractorRationale.c: Electromagnetic frequency is a broader term and does not specifically refer to the photoelectric effect.
distractorRationale.d: Photon frequency is not a standard term used in this context.

questions.stem: Which equation relates the energy of a photon to its frequency?
questions.explanation: The equation E = hf relates the energy (E) of a photon to its frequency (f), where h is Planck's constant. This relationship is fundamental in quantum mechanics and describes how energy is quantized in photons.

distractorRationale.a: E = mc² relates energy to mass, not frequency.
distractorRationale.c: E = mv² is the kinetic energy formula, not applicable here.
distractorRationale.d: E = 1/2 mv² is also related to kinetic energy, not photon energy.
